record_identity.title: Hermes agent ran unattended during intrusion into Thailand’s Ministry of Finance

incident_identity.historical_event_name: Hermes AI-assisted Thailand Ministry of Finance intrusion
incident_identity.date_basis: Hunt.io archived the relevant attack infrastructure from 9–13 July 2026 and published its investigation on 23 July 2026.

summary: Hunt.io and researcher Bob Diachenko reported recovering live attack infrastructure and Hermes agent logs from an intrusion targeting Thailand's Ministry of Finance. The operator configured Hermes in unattended or 'YOLO' mode, bypassing approval prompts, while the agent enumerated ministry systems, assessed privilege-escalation paths and searched files and personnel-record directories. Hunt.io reported evidence of compromise across multiple ministry systems but did not establish the initial-access method or exfiltration of the enumerated office files.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: Hunt.io reports 585 files and 470 MB of attack tooling and stolen credentials across exposed directories, active session material, deployed webshells and internal-network evidence. Recovered Hermes logs show autonomous post-compromise enumeration and privilege-escalation assessment. The operator intentionally enabled unattended execution.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: This is a real-world deployment of an autonomous agent as offensive cyber tooling. Because a hostile operator deliberately disabled approval prompts and supplied the attack objective, the occurrence does not by itself establish an internal governance failure of Hermes; the material governance issue is the availability and operationalisation of unattended agentic capability in a live government intrusion.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The occurrence broadens VIGIL beyond frontier-chatbot failures into open-source agentic cyber operations and provides evidence for future Caelestis controls around unattended execution, tool authority, misuse resistance and operator-configurable safety boundaries.
assessment_boundaries: The initial-access pathway is not established.
Hunt.io did not establish exfiltration of the office and personnel files enumerated by Hermes.
The public evidence does not identify the underlying foundation-model runtime used by Hermes in this operation.
The operator deliberately enabled YOLO mode, so malicious use is not automatically classified as a Hermes governance failure.

That does not yet establish a current VIGIL Failure Class attributable to the agent rather than malicious operator choice.

severity_assessment.materialised_consequence: Recovered evidence indicates compromise of multiple Ministry of Finance systems, active session material, webshell deployment and autonomous internal enumeration by Hermes.
severity_assessment.affected_scope: Thailand Ministry of Finance internal systems identified in the recovered attack infrastructure; the complete number of compromised hosts and affected personnel is not established.
severity_assessment.seriousness_and_persistence: The occurrence involved active compromise of national government financial infrastructure and persistent post-compromise tooling. Public evidence does not establish destructive effects or confirmed exfiltration of the enumerated personnel files.
severity_assessment.quantitative_information: Hunt.io archived 585 files and 470 MB of attack tooling and stolen credentials across three exposed directories and identified five Hermes call-log files tied to ministry post-compromise activity.
severity_assessment.evidentiary_limits: The initial-access pathway is not established. Hunt.io did not establish exfiltration of the office and personnel files enumerated by Hermes. The public evidence does not identify the underlying foundation-model runtime used by Hermes in this operation. The operator deliberately enabled YOLO mode, so malicious use is not automatically classified as a Hermes governance failure.
severity_assessment.band_rationale: S2 rather than S1 is appropriate because the evidence does not establish catastrophic, irreversible or life-threatening harm. S2 rather than S3 is appropriate because active compromise of national-government finance infrastructure with webshells, session material and autonomous internal reconnaissance is a substantial realised security consequence.
